God I hate Gehenna. And Caine. It was a very, very useful little bit of
stupidity back inna date, but WW simply doesn't have a handle on the
concept of a myth. Do you realize that Dark Ages was a *better*
sourcebook because even though Caine's myth was omnipresent, Caine
himself was *not* so the game was playable without vast amounts of
inane plot devices and sanctimonious bs? But I digress.

The Reckoning line in WW was about Hunters. The line presented Hunters
in a rather implausible way as they never had the wherewithal to
organize formally. They were a recent phenomenon, I think brought on by
Gehenna. There is no good reason why they were isolated from Mages as
they have similar abilities -- I think they are all Awakened beings.
(If you don't know WW canon, feel free to ignore this). It made up many
stupid powers for them that did not in any way flow in harmony with any
other systems in WW, but that's how they always work. But the premise
was good: mortals destroying kindred because kindred were bad.
Sometimes they destroy other stuff too, but mostly kindred.

(N.B. The Hunter book, though awful, did kill Wraith, I understand it,
and Wraith was a paragraph's worth of premise then thousands of pages
of suckage, so Hunter did have something going for it.)

Actually, I think this could be a very good set. If the set is about
hunters, it's about allies. Allies could use more support, imo, and
offer a variety of interesting concepts. And mortals really should be
slapping down kindred more often in game; we wouldn't even need the
Masquerade if mortals couldn't do that.

A repeated note to WW: create a way, availible via multiple methods
(Master, action, etc.) to rid the world of an in-play Event. We already
need this, but if the next set *is* about allies, The Unmasking is
going to go from interesting to goddamn nightmare.

Of course, that can be fun in its own right.

-- DoR

Messages.Author: Fabio 'Sooner' Macedo

Do you think so? Dark Ages (at least in its first edition) had not one,
but two books of myth (Erciyes Fragments and Revelations of the Dark
Mother, as opposed to the Book of Nod). Most of the plots used in
Vampire Revised has its roots there. Both the Giovanni and Transilvania
Chronicles beginned around the Dark Ages release, and had the first two
books based on the Dark Ages plotlines - not to mention that they set
stage for future plot devices used in Revised as well.

I didn't read the *revised* Dark Ages line (that one who expanded into
Inquisitors and such), but all I read *about* the line mentions a new
plot device, the War of Princes. Admitelly, it seems to have far more
supplements on Roads and Citybooks than plot-driven books, so maybe
your take on the matter is the fairest. But speaking of the early Dark
Ages line, I see it as the main pool from which most of Gehenna plots
were spawned.

> The Reckoning line in WW was about Hunters. The line presented Hunters
> in a rather implausible way as they never had the wherewithal to
> organize formally. They were a recent phenomenon, I think brought on by
> Gehenna.

Hunter: the Reckoning is like that.

The Year of the Reckoning books presented at least one book for each
gameline (even Wraith: the Oblivion) detailing how mortals deal with
the monsters. In some, the mortals are mostly of the "gifted" sort, but
the general stance is that each book will not cover hunters only. Up to
this moment, we don't know if the set will be based on Hunter: the
Reckoning or the Year of the Reckoning line in general. I hope it's the
latter case - I'm not too fond of god-imbued Hunters spawned from
nowhere as a plot device either.

Though one could argue that this does little difference in light of
VTES rules; any ally released will be far from powerful anyway (if for
nothing else, because they *are allies*, not regular crypt cards), no
matter if it's based on Hunters as in H:tR or regular
mortals/mediums/government goons etc. as in previous supplements. (from
now on, I'll use Hunters with capital H to refer to the latter case).

There is no good reason why they were isolated from Mages as
> they have similar abilities -- I think they are all Awakened beings.
> (If you don't know WW canon, feel free to ignore this). It made up many
> stupid powers for them that did not in any way flow in harmony with any
> other systems in WW, but that's how they always work. But the premise
> was good: mortals destroying kindred because kindred were bad.
> Sometimes they destroy other stuff too, but mostly kindred.

I recall H:tR had a supplement on each supernatural type as the Hunters
view them. Walking Dead for wraiths/risen, Moonstruck for the
werewolves and so on. But everyone I know that played H:tR seems to
believe that the most common foe for the Hunters are the walking dead.
Maybe it's just a personal preference these players/Storytellers share
in common, but I the impression stuck on me.

> Actually, I think this could be a very good set. If the set is about
> hunters, it's about allies. Allies could use more support, imo, and
> offer a variety of interesting concepts. And mortals really should be
> slapping down kindred more often in game; we wouldn't even need the
> Masquerade if mortals couldn't do that.

I don't know if this conforms to existing Masquerade canon. The
Masquerade exists not because any mortal can "slap down" Kindred at
will; it exists because mortals are out there in far superior numbers -
at a 1:10.000 ratio if I remember correctly. Once you get the whole
humanity to set about finding and hunting vampires, then there'll be no
Kindred to tell the tale. The Inquisition worried the Kindred not
because any given individual Inquisitor could enter town and slay alone
every vampire he'd encounter, but because the mere presence of
officials from the order would inspire the locals to search, pinpoint
and set fire on their kindred masters' bodies and havens. And even
then, most of the time it was a result of other vampires' betrayals -
elders throwing neonates "into the fire" so they could gain time to
relocate/reform their ways with more subtetly.

Even the Hunters on H:tR were not that powerful or efficient. Most of
their tactics involve gathering together and striking a single target a
time. They couldn't deal with a horde of Sabbat war cannon fodder, per
example. Or even a single Black Hand or Assamite assassin.
I prefer VTES to abide to that notion - I'm pretty happy with the power
level assinged to most allies in the CCG so far.

> A repeated note to WW: create a way, availible via multiple methods
> (Master, action, etc.) to rid the world of an in-play Event. We already
> need this, but if the next set *is* about allies, The Unmasking is
> going to go from interesting to goddamn nightmare.
> Of course, that can be fun in its own right.
> -- DoR

I don't think it would make that much sense. Gehenna Events are there
to represent global issues that affect anyone and are, for the most
part, cosmic shifts. I don't think any vampire, minion or Methuselah,
should have the power to get rid quickly and easily of such situations.
If he or she could, he or she should be able to win the Jyhad with no
more than a couple of gestures with his or her hand.

You could argue that Events should not have been released at all, but
that's another issue. Going back to power level and playability, I find
the Unmasking to be a poor example of how game-shattering an Event
could be. It grants fixed intercept for more than one minion, sure -
but it gives that permacept to minions which, for the most part, can't
get it transient intercept anywhere else. Not to mention that they are
way easier to get rid of in general (let's forget the dedicated War
Ghoul deck for a while).

All the other potentially game-shattering events require either a heavy
setup or concede its benefits to all players. So most of the time, I
see event-based decks backfiring due to multiple events hard
requirements and extra clauses; decks which include a couple of events
for enhancing the main strategy, but that sometimes end up being foiled
by their own cards (Anthelios and Conquest of Humanity are good
examples of this); or decks relying on one event but that require even
further setup (such as a Wormwood-based Corruption deck, which ends up
needing tons of event just to remove counters from Wormwood). In all
the games I've seen events played, if someone got too screwed up by
them, it was clear that deckbuilding issues were also to blame (such as
a deck that depends too often on hunting to recoup blood being foiled
by Restricted Vitae); when not, focus choice were key to the problem,
and that deck would be screwed up anyway if he had a different predator
(such as weenie vote decks hosed by Nightmares Upon Nightmares, but
they could be screwed up by a number of cards/strategies anyway, from
heavy stealth bleed to Cryptic Mission Machines to other weenie decks).

That noted, let's remember in-play Events have an "easy", global way to
leave the table: oust the player controlling them. If the player
manages to put Events in the table and survive any onslaught, you can't
blame the Events on that. Blame his or her predator's poor ousting
power. :D

best,

Fabio "Sooner" Macedo
Giovanni Newsletter Editor in absentia

money into their last expansion, that DOES affect me. I may not be

bought the new cards - unless I want to consign myself and the

fast, the card design sucked. Not enough real origianl ideas, not
enough time to play test, not enough time to turn around mistakes

properly play tested. The lack of time to market showed.

starting to feel the MTG "funk" starting to creep into VTES. It
started back with KMW and the CE changes in reprint "policies". Plus

new players into the game" is actually working? In my limited corner
of the world, I do not see an increase of new players. In fact, I
believe any increase in new players is balanced by a fading out of
older ones (and I do consider myself an older player). Personally, I
was/am not happy with the release schedule and contents of LoB.

(typically a box of starters and four booster boxes). Thus I wonder
how many new players this order represents? Maybe an average of three
new players would order that amount of product, total? Plus what about
the loyalty factor? How many new players turn into longer term
players? To me most new players show up, perhaps purchase $100 worth
of cards and usually fade away after a couple of months. Meanwhile,
the veteran players drop $250 each expansion year after year as long as
they don't fade away. I guess that my math may be off but I just don't
see the logic in the more expansions = more new players. I also look
at some numbers from the last five years and wonder when we are going
to see the results of all these new sets, when it comes to an increased
player base. It seems to me the year after year this game just slides
along. Never growing to large numbers yet never fully fading away.

somewhere around the country/globe.

that the time between releases is too short-but then want to preorder
four boxes of it anyways. It must be that evaporating UV coating smell

>Expansions that come "too often" are not bad for VTES but MtG scene is
>not developing in Belarus because of rotation and crap cards (caused by
>expansions that come out "too often").

You're confusing M:tG with V:TES too easily.

- Set rotations force you to buy new sets to remain competitive. Your
old cards stop being playable.

- Set rotations often introduce a new mechanic(s) that you must master
to remain competitive.

- New mechanics are often explorer over several releases for the same
set, so you have to buy each of several sets to explore that new
mechanic properly.

In short, you have to buy cards if you want to carry on playing under
the set rotation rules.

In V:TES, that's almost never been the case. Yes, there have been a
couple of occasions where a specific card existed that you really had to
have to compete well - most of which are limited to Ancient Hearts /
Dark Sovereigns. Specifically, I'd list Tomb of Rameses III, Thoughts
Betrayed and Return to Innocence as killer "YOU MUST BUY THIS SET"
cards, once the true abuses of them were well-understood. And each of
these cards was handled once LSJ and WW were able to do so.

Now, assume that you're a player who has a competitive set of decks from
back in the day when you only had Jyhad/V:TES, Dark Sovereigns, Ancient
Hearts and Sabbat to choose from. Can you name any set from White Wolf
that has forced you to buy new cards to remain competitive? Not a set
that has provided new options that could make another strategy more
competitive, just one that you would absolutely need to buy cards from
or DIE IN A HEAP.

Whilst there has been a little tinkering with the rules, the only
substantial new addition is Events and - due to their nature - many,
many decks have trouble coping with them. (This is such that a number
of us have requested new and versatile ways of handling them, myself
included.)

And a good number of truly strong decks from the WotC sets can stand up
to decks even today. Malk Stealth and Bleed has many good options, as
does a solid Ventrue Law Firm, or a Ventrue Obfuscate deck. I've seen
[1/2] Nosferatu Prince decks do very well, and Toreador intercept / gun
decks do rather nicely. Anson heavy master decks are still possible.
The Gangrel Domi/Protean Stanislava / Ingrid Rossler Mind Rape / Grave
Robbing / Bleedzooka Claw deck is still a very strong deck, without too
much modification. You could still put together a strong weenie deck
with Caitiff, Pander and any 2 or 3 cap vampires you had lurking around,
depending on what you wanted to do - weenie vote, weenie bleed etc.

What sets have you been forced to buy to keep up? What decks that you
have have suddenly become worthless due to White Wolf printing new
expansions?

Fabio 'Sooner' Macedo wrote:
> Defender of Ra wrote:
> > God I hate Gehenna. And Caine. It was a very, very useful little bit of
> > stupidity back inna date, but WW simply doesn't have a handle on the
> > concept of a myth. Do you realize that Dark Ages was a *better*
> > sourcebook because even though Caine's myth was omnipresent, Caine
> > himself was *not* so the game was playable without vast amounts of
> > inane plot devices and sanctimonious bs? But I digress.
>
> Do you think so? Dark Ages (at least in its first edition) had not one,
> but two books of myth (Erciyes Fragments and Revelations of the Dark
> Mother, as opposed to the Book of Nod). Most of the plots used in
> Vampire Revised has its roots there.

The myths existed, but the plots were local and immediate. The myths
were not the plot itself.

Gehenna was an entire plot built around a creation story that made no
sense -- in fact, the FoS clanbook made fun of how it made no sense.
"Gee, what you did to your brother was naughty, so I'm going to make
you live forever and give you supernatural powers, but you have to keep
being naughty to survive." I found this laughable in VtM 1st ed. . .
but WW loved it, and it became the metaplot.

An "end times" exclusively for a bunch of amoral parasites is similarly
uncreative and paradoxical. You want an end-times? In the better games
I saw run, "Gehenna" was what happened when some dumbass Sabbat broke
the Masquerade in front of a couple of government agencies and vampires
were, within a decade, rounded up or destroyed. . . and humanity gained
access to supernatural powers en masse as a result of studies upon
their captives. Failure to use these powers wisely starts a
thaumaturgical cataclysm that threatens to destroy Earth. THAT'S
Gehenna.

But I digress.

> Though one could argue that this does little difference in light of
> VTES rules; any ally released will be far from powerful anyway (if for
> nothing else, because they *are allies*, not regular crypt cards),. . .

Noticed that. I am still amused at the fragility of werewolves in this
game. Lupines in the RPG are the GM's way of saying, "You did something
impossibly stupid so now you die." A race of nigh-indestructible,
teleporting, super-strong wizards with invisible allies and free
elder-level Celerity that understands you better than you understand
them and, as it happens, hates you. Meanwhile, a Renegade Garou in the
CCG is a speed bump for a competent combat deck.

I'd say allies are a lot less powerful.

But I understand the mechanical reasons why, and I think that's a
lesser theme issue for Jyhad.

I don't expect the next set will "break" allies. It might be fun if it
tried.

> I recall H:tR had a supplement on each supernatural type as the Hunters
> view them. Walking Dead for wraiths/risen, Moonstruck for the
> werewolves and so on. But everyone I know that played H:tR seems to
> believe that the most common foe for the Hunters are the walking dead.
> Maybe it's just a personal preference these players/Storytellers share
> in common, but I the impression stuck on me.

They are the most common foe, generally. The Risen was an invented
monster that should have never been invented. But Kindred are the
default "problem" in the WW universe. They come up more often than any
other supernatural in the other books because a) they live where you
live and b) they meddle constantly in mortal affairs. And Hunters
should be concentrating on Kindred nearly exclusively. Garou don't need
to kill people -- they can, but it's frowned upon. Kindred kill people
out of hand.

> >And mortals really should be
> > slapping down kindred more often in game; we wouldn't even need the
> > Masquerade if mortals couldn't do that.
>
> I don't know if this conforms to existing Masquerade canon. The
> Masquerade exists not because any mortal can "slap down" Kindred at
> will; it exists because mortals are out there in far superior numbers -
> at a 1:10.000 ratio if I remember correctly.

That is somewhat incorrect. Do recall that the Inquisition was not
about Europe rising up against Cainites. It was about a small,
dedicated group burning out established vampires with terrifying
accuracy, especially considering their ignorance about their quarry. A
small group of hunters can wipe out the vampires in a city, easily,
with modern weaponry. More importantly, a *rich* group of hunters can
locate those kindred with some hard work (violence is the easy part).
Daylight is a big help in these endeavors.

Kindred physical prowess, by the way, is overrated in the modern day. A
kid with a AK and a decent willpower can torporize most Kindred.
Violence is what happens when you screw up the Jyhad. The CCG is much
more violent than the RPG (when the latter isn't played by munchkins).
Kindred power is in hiding. If a vampire can't hide, 10 guys with a
shovel can drag him screaming into the sun.

Of course, you're right in that if Earth discovers vampires en masse,
they are doomed to scientist cages. Serves them right. :-)

And one more problem: the holy. True Faith is a big deal in Dark Ages,
mostly because there aren't guns. But True Faith humans with guns would
be a bigger threat than Garou for vampires. And if people start to
realize there are vampires about, they might start to believe. That's
what scared the elders in Dark Ages in the old sourcebooks: True Faith
mortals rising up and burning them.

> > A repeated note to WW: create a way, availible via multiple methods
> > (Master, action, etc.) to rid the world of an in-play Event.

> I don't think it would make that much sense. Gehenna Events are there
> to represent global issues that affect anyone and are, for the most
> part, cosmic shifts.

They are shifts so dramatic that it takes a whole discard phase action
to put them into play. Please. The low-level Gehenna Events can be more
devastating to the table than some of the high-level ones. So long as
the cost of an anti-Event card is balanced, it is fine mechanically.
Thematically speaking, if one wanted to be rigid about flavor, Gehenna
Events should develop over the course of a game AND be impossible to
get rid of once in play -- pushing a Methuselah out of the Jyhad will
not stop the Wrath of God. Of course, Gehenna is a poor theme, anyway,
like the insane street preacher with a 10-year old sign reading, "the
world ends this Thursday!" (In fact, one wonders why one of the Gehenna
Events wouldn't end the game.) It is good that the theme is not done to
completiong, both because it's a theme that doesn't deserve support and
because of the obvious mechanical flaws. The notion that Gehenna Events
need to be strong is silly to me.

> I don't think any vampire, minion or Methuselah,
> should have the power to get rid quickly and easily of such situations.
> If he or she could, he or she should be able to win the Jyhad with no
> more than a couple of gestures with his or her hand.

Right, so what of the power of a Methuselah who *starts* Gehenna with a
wave of its hand? You already have that absurdity in-game. Gehenna
cannot mean the end of the world -- it can represent strife and
tribulation, but it's as stupid an armageddon in the CCG as it is in
the RPG, if not more.

> Going back to power level and playability, I find
> the Unmasking to be a poor example of how game-shattering an Event
> could be.

That was my point. I was tongue-in-cheek there. There is no way for the
Unmasking to be broken. I was hoping WW would try in amusement.

> That noted, let's remember in-play Events have an "easy", global way to
> leave the table: oust the player controlling them.

That's hardly an interesting in-game dynamic. That's not a counter at
all. If I can oust you, I will. If I can't, I don't. I've played in
other multiplayer games where there was a card type that couldn't be
removed easily. . . but its player could. It led to stupid,
uninteresting situations where you'd throw the balance of power out the
window and eliminate someone because one global effect they threw out,
offhand, was ruining your day.

Global effects need to be checked far more than, say, Locations,
because of their ability to shape the table. (Of course, Locations with
global effects can be easily checked.)

-- DoR

Messages.Author: Defender of Ra
Messages.Body:
CthuluKitty wrote:

> Different groups had their own
> interpretations of when Gehenna would come, what the signs of it would
> be, if those signs were present, or if Gehenna was a ridiculous myth
> altogether. I personally liked this take on the World of Darkness much
> more than what WW did in 3rd edition. The situation in Mage was even
> worse IMO.

Mage's problems was far mor basic:
· Magick, if used intelligently, had no discernable limits for even a
starting character.
· Vampires couldn't exist.

I'll leave the first point out as a naked, unsubstantiated assertion
since it gets us more off-topic than normal. But the latter was more
telling. The Technocracy hates vampires. The Technocracy pretty much
controls the world. (Please don't post examples of where it's weak,
etc. -- I know it isn't absolute -- the premise is that it is running
the show and the Traditions are rebels.)

Kindred want and need power for fun and survival. They control
governments.
The Technocracy needs to control humanity to succeed. It controls
governments.
And, finally, the Technocracy has better super-powers than the Kindred.

There's simply no reason why the Camarilla, et. al., would be around in
Mage. If I give Technocrat players five minutes they're whuppn' up on
elder vampires in no time. After all, Tradition mages sit on their
asses complaining about the good old days. Methselahs make countries go
to war with each other over spite. Kindred would be purged. Easily.

VtM, for all its faults, was simply the best sourcebook WW put out.
Instead of having to invent stuff to explain stupidity, you could just
throw stupidity out. Didn't like a clan? Throw it out. Mage, on the
other hand, had concept problems at its core that you couldn't get
past. . . unless your players were twits who wanted to blow stuff up
and/or have sex with whatever didn't get blown up. Five minutes of
thought broke that game down. I watched it happen.

-- DoR

Messages.Body:
Gregory Stuart Pettigrew wrote:
> On Fri, 9 Dec 2005, Defender of Ra wrote:
> Yeah. The Renegade Garou says to himself, "Wait, why am I helping these
> vampires again?" and leaves.

. . . but not before taking a Gangrel's head as a souvenir. It *is* a
servant of the Wyrm, after all.

> Oh, and about the Technocracy. The Technocracy doesn't really care about
> Vampires because Vampires don't, as a rule, make war on reality. As a
> matter of fact, most Vampires, particularly the Camarilla, help enforce
> it.

Vampires are Reality Deviants. Though they do help maintain the
Paradigm in their own way, they still violate the same by merely
existing. Worse, within their circles, they commit a variety of vulgar
activities. (The fact that they kill and abuse humans is also mildly
troubling, I'm sure.) And do keep in mind not all vampires uphold the
Masquerade -- which, of course, is a serious plot problem, as I
mentioned.

More important are issues of *control.* You are right in that Kindred
seem less threatening than, say Changlings (God I hate tho -- eh, we'll
save that rant). But Kindred commit the unthinkable sin of being
active. There is no good reason why a vampire wouldn't try to blood
bond every senator, the president, and all of the supremes if he could.
The only forces who would be able to stop him are a) other Kindred (who
are doing the same thing) and b) Technocrats.

The Technocracy isn't as concerned with vampiric vulgarity as it is
with vampiric activities. As soon as you run a game with both factions
acting intelligently, you end up with an all-out war. And the Kindred
will lose.

Nothing counters Prime 5.

I do think that non-Mage magicians of the more conventional sort add a
lot to the background of Vampire. Competent mortals are neat. I felt
the same way about Lupines -- Garou were simply too much for a game of
Vampire, but powerful, enigmatic Lupines (sans teleportation, etc.)
were fine. Great, even. Another reason to join the Cam -- they might
help protect you from random Lupine assaults. (That was how it was in
games I influenced, at least.)

(Garou bring up another problem in WW canon, btw: there's virtually no
stopping an intelligent Glass Walker from annihilating the Kindred,
especially with help from friends. A race of invisible allies that can
follow vampires around and manipulate them is a bit much. The games
worked better as stand-alone than as cosmopolitan affairs.)

-- DoR

Local and immediate? I believe you are referring to Gehenna plots
within the books released near the end of Revised. That I understand.
But even then, a good number of them were related to myths as they've
shown up in these two books I've mentioned, written on Dark Ages
vampires' perspective and readings on the Book of Nod.

Usually I'd say that one could saw that coming since 2nd edition at
least - once the setting came closer to Gehenna, obviously some things
would get strange just so players and Storytellers alike would be
caught off balance, and it could lead to a few exaggerations. But the
core problem was there since 1st Edition. No matter how personal most
books from the beginning were, the concept of Gehenna and impending
doom was released there.

> Gehenna was an entire plot built around a creation story that made no
> sense -- in fact, the FoS clanbook made fun of how it made no sense.
> "Gee, what you did to your brother was naughty, so I'm going to make
> you live forever and give you supernatural powers, but you have to keep
> being naughty to survive." I found this laughable in VtM 1st ed. . .
> but WW loved it, and it became the metaplot.

Oh, so you're talking about metaplot as a whole. I understand that, and
we both know you're not the only one. I do liked metaplot, but mostly
didn't use it. I saw it as a side bonus I'd get when buying gaming
books - so if I never used metaplot content, it would made for
something interesting to read at least.
Of course, that tidbit is a matter of preference. Some plots I liked,
some not.

And we can safely say that even WW knew it got a little over the top,
since the nWoD doesn't have metaplot at all.

> An "end times" exclusively for a bunch of amoral parasites is similarly
> uncreative and paradoxical.

"Uncreative" is a matter of opinion. But how paradoxical? One could
argue that the mere existence of a good bunch of parasites inbetween
humanity for so much time without being discovered is paradoxical. I
see this as poetic liberty necessary for a little fun in the stories -
to make players never feel truly safe no matter how many contacts,
allies and raw power the acquire during play. Sounds fair.

But then again, nWoD is there to offer an alternative. No end times. No
fixed myth of creation and such.

You want an end-times? In the better games
> I saw run, "Gehenna" was what happened when some dumbass Sabbat broke
> the Masquerade in front of a couple of government agencies and vampires
> were, within a decade, rounded up or destroyed. . . and humanity gained
> access to supernatural powers en masse as a result of studies upon
> their captives. Failure to use these powers wisely starts a
> thaumaturgical cataclysm that threatens to destroy Earth. THAT'S
> Gehenna.

I believe one or two Gehenna scenarios in the last book offered such a
story, if you drop down the "humanity with supernatural powers due to
post research" part. That means the designers considered this
possibility, even when metaplot began its course.

> > I recall H:tR had a supplement on each supernatural type as the Hunters
> > view them. Walking Dead for wraiths/risen, Moonstruck for the
> > werewolves and so on. But everyone I know that played H:tR seems to
> > believe that the most common foe for the Hunters are the walking dead.
> > Maybe it's just a personal preference these players/Storytellers share
> > in common, but I the impression stuck on me.
>

> monster that should have never been invented.

It seems that the Orpheus designer thought similarly to you. There's no
Risen unless one or two clever Spectre goes down on a projectors' empty
body and went on a rampage. (in case you don't know Orpheus, projectors
are mortals who can will their souls to travel to the afterlife, much
like astral projection).

Have you checked on that line? Orpheus has a very, very different take
on the afterlife even if the line ends has some ties to Wraith (and
none of these is related to political issues). It trimmed down the
original setting to the basics and added a good x-files feel to it,
since it deals with mortals approaching the afterlife and not the other
way round. I loved it, even as I loved Wraith - it's good to have a
very different take to play with ghosts.

But Kindred are the
> default "problem" in the WW universe. They come up more often than any
> other supernatural in the other books because a) they live where you
> live and b) they meddle constantly in mortal affairs. And Hunters
> should be concentrating on Kindred nearly exclusively. Garou don't need
> to kill people -- they can, but it's frowned upon. Kindred kill people
> out of hand.

b) is nice and I can see how Kindred *should* be the main antagonist.
But in practice it wasn't, and a) seems to me a somewhat hindsight
reasoning. Risen live where mortals live. Mages and Wraiths (for the
most part) too, even Mummies. Changelings and Werewolves are the
exception, and even a portion of them live with humans.

The issue is what they can face, not what should be the first or second
target for them (Hunters). They are as ignorant about the supernatural
as any non-Imbued mortal can be.

> > I don't know if this conforms to existing Masquerade canon. The
> > Masquerade exists not because any mortal can "slap down" Kindred at
> > will; it exists because mortals are out there in far superior numbers -
> > at a 1:10.000 ratio if I remember correctly.
>
> That is somewhat incorrect. Do recall that the Inquisition was not
> about Europe rising up against Cainites. It was about a small,
> dedicated group burning out established vampires with terrifying
> accuracy, especially considering their ignorance about their quarry.

It depends on the take a Storyteller chooses on the issue. We have
hints that vampires guided the Inquisition at some point, though
obviously not much (due to reasons you point out, like True Faith's
dangers and such).

A
> small group of hunters can wipe out the vampires in a city, easily,
> with modern weaponry. More importantly, a *rich* group of hunters can
> locate those kindred with some hard work (violence is the easy part).
> Daylight is a big help in these endeavors.
> Kindred physical prowess, by the way, is overrated in the modern day. A
> kid with a AK and a decent willpower can torporize most Kindred.
> Violence is what happens when you screw up the Jyhad. The CCG is much
> more violent than the RPG (when the latter isn't played by munchkins).
> Kindred power is in hiding. If a vampire can't hide, 10 guys with a
> shovel can drag him screaming into the sun.

It still has to do with numbers. The same Kid can't do the same to all
vampires in his city, and you'd still need 10 Hunters with weaponry to
take down all of them - provided they *can locate all of them and
approach in a one-by-one basis*. I didn't read the Hunter gameline, but
all the references to (imbued) Hunters in vampire books made that clear
- they have to fear Hunters because (a) they can attack you in groups
(b) you Kindred don't really know what they are and (c) they have
daylight to act. If you Kindred don't stroll alone, don't leave your
Haven unguarded by ghouls or traps or something and take measures to
not be found, you're safe for the most part.

If it was so easy to hunt vampires, even for the Imbued, how come the
Inquisition/Society of Leopold didn't wipe them out of existence
before?

I believe most of the time, this approach on Hunters (even the Imbued
ones) has much to do with storytellers' and players' expectations that
hunting Kindred would be too much fun. This leads to a somewhat
optimistic take on what hunters can do, and to an unrealistic view - as
unealistic and uncreative as any plot WW has ever released.

> Of course, you're right in that if Earth discovers vampires en masse,
> they are doomed to scientist cages. Serves them right. :-)

Of course :)

> And one more problem: the holy. True Faith is a big deal in Dark Ages,
> mostly because there aren't guns. But True Faith humans with guns would
> be a bigger threat than Garou for vampires. And if people start to
> realize there are vampires about, they might start to believe. That's
> what scared the elders in Dark Ages in the old sourcebooks: True Faith
> mortals rising up and burning them.

But even at that time True Faith was all so rare. People could be
superstitious, but they were living a harsher life than we have today.
But again, I believe it's a matter of what take a Storyteller wants to
have on the subject. Myself, I never used a NPC with True Faith because
none of the stories I've ran had a situation where a character with
True Faith appearing would've made sense. They're rare, so if I was to
use them, I'd better include some plot where the Inquisition was
involved, or that happened in a major european city, which was not the
case.

> Thematically speaking, if one wanted to be rigid about flavor, Gehenna
> Events should develop over the course of a game

Most do. To get the full reward of a Gehenna event, usually you have to
build a deck toward the goal of building up events over gameplay.

You say that even the ones that do not require Gehenna events in the
table to function can be game-shattering. I'm still not convinced of
that. Blood Trade only affects decks that play Boons. Restricted Vitae
only affects decks that *depend* on hunting, and there's plenty of
other effects that give you blood (I personally think that decks that
*depend* on hunting have serious problems, even when no Gehenna event
is in play). Thirst needs more events in play to be effective,
otherwise it affects 1-caps only. The same goes for Nightmares Upon
Nightmares. And Anthelios is strong, but it also helps your opponents.
A single Minion Tap brought back by your prey can save him or her from
ousting, and if you've played Anthelios, it's your responsability.
The only exception is Unmasking, but I've already talked about it.

AND be impossible to
> get rid of once in play -- pushing a Methuselah out of the Jyhad will
> not stop the Wrath of God.

That's why I mentioned the 'oust them' possibility. If even ousting a
Methuselah would not be thematically apropriate, how come a mere master
or library card would be enough?
We already gained Not to Be, which I find to be the most appropriate
way to represent such an endevour - the event was bound to happen, but
by some strange twist of fate, it didn't.

I'd say that the designers already had made quite a stretch by creating
ADV Jan's special, Black Hand Ritual, Emergency Preparations and Not to
Be as means to deal with Events.

Of course, Gehenna is a poor theme, anyway,
> like the insane street preacher with a 10-year old sign reading, "the
> world ends this Thursday!" (In fact, one wonders why one of the Gehenna
> Events wouldn't end the game.) It is good that the theme is not done to
> completiong, both because it's a theme that doesn't deserve support and
> because of the obvious mechanical flaws. The notion that Gehenna Events
> need to be strong is silly to me.

But they aren't. They have serious playability issues, they require
quite a setup, and if you use them in a drop-one-or-two basis, they
aren't more game-shattering than, say, you sitting next to a combat
deck when you have only 5x Dodges as combat defense.

I would like to see someone providing a good example on how a single
event can be game-shattering without a careful setup. In my playgroup,
few people use them for playability reasons. Everytime I saw a deck
being hosed by Events, usually that was because the Event in question
just brought up a vey serious deckbuilding flaw - like a Tremere deck
with not enough combat trying to push actions at 1-stealth only facing
a Shambling Hordes or War Ghoul deck with Unmasking in play. I wouldn't
blame the Unmasking on this case.

Of course, one could argue that Events affect *everyone* on the table,
not just you if you sit next to the *wrong* deck. But even then, the
flaws on deckbuilding are there. Sometimes the same problems could
arise from a cross-table deal or other card that goes around the table,
from Anarch Troublemaker or Millicent Smith. That's why I ask of all of
you who feels Events are bad for the game to tell me your stories.
Maybe I'm doubtful because not many people play Events in here...

> Right, so what of the power of a Methuselah who *starts* Gehenna with a
> wave of its hand? You already have that absurdity in-game.

No, no vampire starts the Event. Otherwise they would be Master cards.
That's why a new cardtype was invented - to represent a situation no
methuselah or minion in the game could handle alone.
That's why the counter-events are quite a stretch, moved by game rules
issues, moreso than the Events themselves.

> > That noted, let's remember in-play Events have an "easy", global way to
> > leave the table: oust the player controlling them.
>
> That's hardly an interesting in-game dynamic. That's not a counter at
> all. If I can oust you, I will. If I can't, I don't.

But this game in particular has other in-game mechanics to help you
with that: its multiplayer-oriented nature.
Usually, when a player affects the whole table with a host of events,
it will get way easier to amass allies to gang on the event player.

I've played in
> other multiplayer games where there was a card type that couldn't be
> removed easily. . . but its player could. It led to stupid,
> uninteresting situations where you'd throw the balance of power out the
> window and eliminate someone because one global effect they threw out,
> offhand, was ruining your day.

I don't see a problem with that. How different it is from 3 players
ganging up on the one who has vote lock, or when he or she is playing
sneak bleed and they don't have enough intercept?

On the other hands, how many times a War Ghoul deck with Unmasking is
left alone because any other player has some means to deal with it?
(blocking the recruiting of the WGs, lots of Fortitude, ally-stealing
cards, ousting the player before he could torporize all your vampires
etc.)

> Global effects need to be checked far more than, say, Locations,
> because of their ability to shape the table. (Of course, Locations with
> global effects can be easily checked.)

I still need an example to be convinced... Sure there's more ways to
burn/steal a location than there is to get rid of Events, but they
don't show up that often. Some locations can be key for the GW a player
acquires, specially votey ones. How come an Event that usually affects
its wielder as much as the rest of the table can be worse?

best,

Fabio "Sooner" Macedo

Messages.Author: Defender of Ra
Messages.Body:
Fabio 'Sooner' Macedo wrote:
> Changing subject since it's so off-topic.

> Local and immediate? I believe you are referring to Gehenna plots
> within the books released near the end of Revised. That I understand.
> But even then, a good number of them were related to myths as they've
> shown up in these two books I've mentioned, written on Dark Ages
> vampires' perspective and readings on the Book of Nod.

Ah, but relationship is not *determinative*. Sure, plots involved old
vampires screwing around, but they were specific vampires living in
specific, geographical locales involved in local politics with a
consistent history associated with that area. . .

You see the difference between that and "Antedeluvian X wakes up and,
generically, many vampires in a generic location are agitated"?

The former is a gamebook. The latter is an internet discussion that was
passed off as a gamebook. And, in the latter, the only two options for
the WW writers were to a) reestablish the status quo or b) change the
line forever. They were never willing to do (b) and so (a) was
inevitable. One of the reasons why the line was uncreative when Gehenna
came in.

I recall the Nosferatu Antie waking up and nuclear weapons getting
involved. Don't worry: it was all settled by the end of the scenario,
like a Simpsons episode (which parodies normal sitcoms).

Calling vampires Cainites can add flavor. Having vamires deal with
fallout from Caine's activities is dumb. Flavor is fine, so long as it
doesn't eat immediate plotlines.

> Oh, so you're talking about metaplot as a whole. I understand that, and
> we both know you're not the only one. I do liked metaplot, but mostly
> didn't use it. I saw it as a side bonus I'd get when buying gaming
> books - so if I never used metaplot content, it would made for
> something interesting to read at least.

After a point, the metaplot began to eat up resources better used to
establish world depth. Dark Age worldbooks gave you a better feel and
presence in the geographical climes described because, I argue, in
part, Caine wasn't the point.

> "Uncreative" is a matter of opinion.

Not completely. A sufficient degree of imitation can be deemed
"uncreative". In fact, if you're stepping on someone's copyrights in a
genre, uncreativity can have legal effect. (Games Workshop once sued
Blizzard over Orcs.) Though I'll concede it's a very fuzzy thing.

> But how paradoxical? One could
> argue that the mere existence of a good bunch of parasites inbetween
> humanity for so much time without being discovered is paradoxical.

"Good" parasites? I think you're referring to a part of Gehenna's story
that I missed.

> I
> see this as poetic liberty necessary for a little fun in the stories -
> to make players never feel truly safe no matter how many contacts,
> allies and raw power the acquire during play. Sounds fair.

I did that by having humans rise up and kill them. Then, to keep the
knowlege of Kindred existence from spreading, a Camarilla "cleanup
crew" (a concept that I never saw in the books but might have been
written about in some of the later stuff) would show up and burn out
any sign of vampiric activity, up to and including destruction of
financial and political entities backed by Kindred. All mortals
involved would be killed (rare -- this aggravates the problem) or
bought off for huge sums and/or mind controlled. Kindred found to be a
threat to the Masquerade were summarially executed by terrified and
terribly strong Archons backed by two to three Justicars.

Screw Gehenna. You put the threat of death before a vampire at the
hands of the entire planet, and they'll toe the line.

> But then again, nWoD is there to offer an alternative. No end times. No
> fixed myth of creation and such.

And nWoD has its own problems that we need not get into.

> You want an end-times? In the better games
> > I saw run, "Gehenna" was what happened when some dumbass Sabbat broke

> > the Masquerade in front of a couple of government agencies...

> I believe one or two Gehenna scenarios in the last book offered such a
> story, if you drop down the "humanity with supernatural powers due to
> post research" part. That means the designers considered this
> possibility, even when metaplot began its course.

If they had taken the Sabbat seriously, that scenario would have
happened before 1400 AD.

> It seems that the Orpheus designer thought similarly to you. There's no
> Risen unless one or two clever Spectre goes down on a projectors' empty
> body and went on a rampage. (in case you don't know Orpheus, projectors
> are mortals who can will their souls to travel to the afterlife, much
> like astral projection).
>
> Have you checked on that line? Orpheus has a very, very different take
> on the afterlife even if the line ends has some ties to Wraith (and
> none of these is related to political issues). It trimmed down the
> original setting to the basics and added a good x-files feel to it,
> since it deals with mortals approaching the afterlife and not the other
> way round. I loved it, even as I loved Wraith - it's good to have a
> very different take to play with ghosts.

Orpheus actually sounds more like Delta Green. That's a modern-day Call
of Cthulhu line.

> But Kindred are the
> > default "problem" in the WW universe. They come up more often than any
> > other supernatural in the other books because a) they live where you
> > live and b) they meddle constantly in mortal affairs.

> b) is nice and I can see how Kindred *should* be the main antagonist.
> But in practice it wasn't, and a) seems to me a somewhat hindsight
> reasoning. Risen live where mortals live. Mages and Wraiths (for the
> most part) too, even Mummies. Changelings and Werewolves are the
> exception, and even a portion of them live with humans.

Garou and Changelings have their own, introverted societies. (The
former shouldn't, really, but that's a different rant.) It's back to
what I said before: taking WW canon at face value, a Kindred should
have the POTUS Dominated and Blood Bonded. A Kindred should have the
same done to your mayor. Hell, to many on the city council. The Bloods
and the Crips should probably be a front for a couple of Kindred.
They're a conspiracy made plausible (using the term loosely) via super
powers.

Hunters will deal with Kindred more often b/c Kindred interefere more
with human lives than Garou et. al. This actually happens in tabletop.
Werewolf games often involve no Sleeper contact of significance
_at_all_. Mage society is fairly insular -- you can spend all your time
in the Umbra just to avoid paradox. And Mages don't want to eat people.
They don't commit assault, battery, rape, and grand larceny just to
survive. Their conspiracy looks more like a social club.

We can agree to disagree -- I admit this is a fuzzy concept. But from
both canon AND the way an average game is run, vampire is going to have
a player deal with mortals day in and day out. The other games might
not even find you on Earth.

> The issue is what they can face, not what should be the first or second
> target for them (Hunters). They are as ignorant about the supernatural
> as any non-Imbued mortal can be.

Built-in supernatural senses will fix that, won't it? What happens when
a race of mortals learns how to tell vampires in a crowd, unerringly?
You get a massacre (of mortals) or a war.

> > That is somewhat incorrect. Do recall that the Inquisition was not
> > about Europe rising up against Cainites. It was about a small,
> > dedicated group burning out established vampires with terrifying
> > accuracy, especially considering their ignorance about their quarry.
>
> It depends on the take a Storyteller chooses on the issue. We have
> hints that vampires guided the Inquisition at some point, though
> obviously not much (due to reasons you point out, like True Faith's
> dangers and such).

We are both right. It's not a hint, either; the old Ventrue clanbook
mentions a Kindred starting the Inquisition to get at his foes. The
Lasombra were WAAAAY to close to the church. It backfired. A bunch of
guys with True Faith burned them out (iirc) in the church, and then
used their newfound knowledge from tortured vamps to go on a rampage or
two.

You are right that True Faith's power is dependent on the Storyteller.
. . but it's also dependent upon players.

A smart player who realizes that Faith can be developed and supported
by exposure to the supernatural could seek to "harvest" Faith by
encouraging some mortals to believe. This is doable under WW mechanics.
The results would be. . . unpleasant for Kindred. So it's player and
Storyteller, both.

> It still has to do with numbers. The same Kid can't do the same to all
> vampires in his city, and you'd still need 10 Hunters with weaponry to
> take down all of them - provided they *can locate all of them and
> approach in a one-by-one basis*.

Not a problem. The strength of the Kindred is in ghouls and retainers.
If we "real world" this, you always end up with groups fighting groups.

The Kindred have another problem: the Masquerade. If a Hunter is a part
of a government agency, they have problems. If Hunters make a lot of
noise, they have problems. The Hunters just need to make noise. Blow up
a building, get vampires on tape, show anomalous patterns of
blood-borne disease spread. . . an individual Kindred who survives a
Hunter attack may be taken down by Archons for being too "noisy."

> If you Kindred don't stroll alone, don't leave your
> Haven unguarded by ghouls or traps or something and take measures to
> not be found, you're safe for the most part.

I agree. Again, Kindred are strong because they *hide*. Presence and
Auspex are the power Disciplines. Potence is a sucker's bet.

> If it was so easy to hunt vampires, even for the Imbued, how come the
> Inquisition/Society of Leopold didn't wipe them out of existence
> before?

Kindred did what they did best: manipulate. They bribed and influenced
the powers that be through mortal agents. (You don't want to get too
close to Inquisitors b/c of possible True Faith.) They created mundane
fallout to the Inquisition: do recall that it existed to stamp out
heresy, and that ruffled feathers (and started wars). They purged their
ranks of "noisy" kindred. Then they went balls-to-the-wall: they
created a massive, worldwide conspiracy dedicated to encouraging
*secularism* AND forced every one of their kind to hide in the shadows
upon pain of death.

That's a pretty big reaction to the Society of Leopold. An effective
one, too.

There was fallout from that decision. Emphasis on science has given the
kine the ability to slaughter them more effectively than ever before.
That's the irony of modern VtM: the Kindred have mopped themselves into
a corner.

> I believe most of the time, this approach on Hunters (even the Imbued
> ones) has much to do with storytellers' and players' expectations that
> hunting Kindred would be too much fun. This leads to a somewhat
> optimistic take on what hunters can do, and to an unrealistic view - as
> unealistic and uncreative as any plot WW has ever released.

Optimistic. . . ummmm. . . okay, you will take out the first couple of
Kindred, probably neonates -- maaaybe a Prince or ancilla, but I doubt
it. Nevertheless, you will get in some kills. You're unexpected.

Then the Prince has exactly two options (if he's alive):

Eliminate the Hunters or run for his life.

The latter is required because if he doesn't solve the problem, he has
failed the Masquerade. . . and the Archons will NOT be forgiving.

The Cam will come in and ruin credit card ratings, screw up mortgages,
blood bond, dominate, blackmail, assassinate, intimidate, bribe, kidnap
and extort their way through the Hunter ranks. Look, it's not "Hunter
v. the Prince." Hunters can actually win that war. Princes are really,
really strong in many cases, but smart Hunters want to blow the lid on
vamps -- and the NSA and the CDC are all ears. The Hunters have the
initiative, though they are ignorant and crunchy. AND the Society of
Leopold may catch up with noisy Hunters and start to clue them in. . .
the Prince has a serious problem. Very serious.

The Camarilla, a worldwide conspiracy with assets in the trillions, has
an annoyance. They can solve the problem. And if the Prince can't solve
the problem, he, too, can be solved.

That isn't optimistic. That's a cycle of despair. If I'm running a
Hunter game, I HAVE to clue the PCs into vampiric society early. If I
don't, and I even roughly follow canon, the Cam will come down on the
PCs.

And they will lose. Do not pass go. Do not collect $200.

The Cam cannot allow Hunters a foothold. If it means they have to spend
$100k for every dollar of Hunter equipment and effort, they'll do it in
a heartbeat.

Smart Hunters would be forced to act quietly enough to keep the
Illuminati (that's what we're talking about here) from slaying them.
Then they have to blow the lid on vamps without getting intercepted by
a Kindred pawn in government. It would be a high-stakes, tense
thriller.

I wouldn't call it optimistic, though.

> > And one more problem: the holy. True Faith is a big deal in Dark Ages,
> > mostly because there aren't guns. But True Faith humans with guns would
> > be a bigger threat than Garou for vampires. And if people start to
> > realize there are vampires about, they might start to believe. That's
> > what scared the elders in Dark Ages in the old sourcebooks: True Faith
> > mortals rising up and burning them.
>
> But even at that time True Faith was all so rare. People could be
> superstitious, but they were living a harsher life than we have today.
> But again, I believe it's a matter of what take a Storyteller wants to
> have on the subject.

You're right in that it's Storyteller fiat. The reason for that is the
canon *changed*. True Faith was a detail, a sidenote in VtM. In Dark
Ages it developed systems, systems that made Faith reliable and
replicable, in essence. That's a big, big difference.

> Restricted Vitae
> only affects decks that *depend* on hunting, and there's plenty of
> other effects that give you blood (I personally think that decks that
> *depend* on hunting have serious problems, even when no Gehenna event
> is in play).

Not in my experience. The point of RV is to *force* hunting. I've only
seen it used in FoS and Tremere blood assault decks. Trust me, the
entire table had to hunt after getting a workover from those. RV dooms
some players to ouster when one of those decks hits. If you "splash" RV
in, sure, it's a detail. But if you're already hurting blood supply. .
.

> We already gained Not to Be, which I find to be the most appropriate
> way to represent such an endevour - the event was bound to happen, but
> by some strange twist of fate, it didn't.

No thematic reason for its existance. Methuselah shouldn't be able to
trigger the Wrath of God. They certainly shouldn't be able to stop it.

> I'd say that the designers already had made quite a stretch by creating
> ADV Jan's special, Black Hand Ritual, Emergency Preparations and Not to
> Be as means to deal with Events.

Limited to very narrow decktypes or low playability, all.

> > The notion that Gehenna Events
> > need to be strong is silly to me.
>
> But they aren't. They have serious playability issues, they require

> quite a setup. . .

Not all, I think. Uncanceallbility is strong in and of itself. I think
that the key to using Events is to have a strong, core concept that
uses Events to aggravate one's advantage. The Unmasking is weak because
allies are weak. It's only good as an enabler, imo. Knocking out the
Cam or Sabbat or, as I mentioned above, using Restricted Vitae well can
boost an already decent or strong deck. It's a low-cost play with broad
effects.

Again, I don't think Gehenna Events are *too* powerful. I think:
1) They would have to be more significant and less controllable to be
thematic and
1a) it's good that they are weak, thematically, or they'd hurt the game
if they were stronger and
1b) it's a stupid theme, anyway, so good riddance.
2) Because they are a strong (not overstrong) game concept, and are
pretty generically playable, they should have more generic counters.

> No, no vampire starts the Event. Otherwise they would be Master cards.

Actions aren't Master cards but represent Methuselah manipulations.
"Hm," says Nefertiti. "I think I shall use Legal Manipulations to screw
up those bank records. I don't know why, but it sounds fun."

> That's why a new cardtype was invented - to represent a situation no
> methuselah or minion in the game could handle alone.

Methuselah put Events into play with less effort than used to play
actions. They can handle them fine.

> > > Events have an "easy", global way to
> > > leave the table: oust the player controlling them.
> >
> > That's hardly an interesting in-game dynamic. That's not a counter at
> > all.
>

> But this game in particular has other in-game mechanics to help you
> with that: its multiplayer-oriented nature.

We will have to agree to disagree. I've played LOTS of multiplayer
games and I find vampire politics to be unsophisticated compared to
some of those -- gauche in a few cases. Vampire has a better
multiplayer mechanic than most -- pred-prey is an innovation. But INWO,
for example, is a much more terrifying of players cooperating to beat
another down. I've played games where deals are essential to victory. I
could be mute all game in Jyhad and sweep.

>
> I've played in
> > other multiplayer games where there was a card type that couldn't be
> > removed easily. . . but its player could. It led to stupid,
> > uninteresting situations where you'd throw the balance of power out the
> > window and eliminate someone because one global effect they threw out,
> > offhand, was ruining your day.
>
> I don't see a problem with that. How different it is from 3 players
> ganging up on the one who has vote lock, or when he or she is playing
> sneak bleed and they don't have enough intercept?

You are confusing cardtype with deck strategy. If I put out ONE card
and now I must die because of that ONE card, it is a vastly different
situation than where I must die because my deck is an Unholy
Overpowered Designer-Loves-Me Cheese, for example. The latter is
acceptable. The former is not.

> > Global effects need to be checked far more than, say, Locations,
> > because of their ability to shape the table. (Of course, Locations with
> > global effects can be easily checked.)
>

> I still need an example to be convinced...How come an Event that usually affects

> its wielder as much as the rest of the table can be worse?

You really haven't seen Restricted Vitae work well, have you? :-) If an
Event is used well, it doesn't affect its controller at all.

-- DoR

>

When a relic nuke detonated in Enoch, and a second in the Labyrinth,
the last Great Maelstrom in the Shadowlands shunted hundreds upon
thousands of Wraiths back into the skinlands -- this is chronicled in
Ends of Empire, the last book in the Wraith line.

Some beings who work for the Powers That Be looked down shortly after,
said "holy shit, when did that happen?" and bonked a number of mortals
with somewhat-divine powers to find and destroy these anomalies. They
had the somewhat unanticipated effect of allowing them to also find and
harm vampires, shapeshifters, mages, and the like. Thi is chronicled
in the book that came with the Hunter Storyteller Screen (or maybe the
Storytellers guide, i can't remember).

Thus, the reason most players assume the Hunter's primary role is the
hunt the walking dead is, well, because it is. Hunter: The Reckoning
is Army of Darkness the RPG, as written (poorly) by White Wolf.

Interesting notes about the crappiness that was Hunter:
1) Each groups line of powers had an uber-cheesy fifth dot that, by the
rules presented in the core book, could not ever be attained. I heard
that a book eventually did come out saying how these powers were
learned two years later, but by then I had long given up on the line.
2) The guidlines for making baddies for your Hunters to kill pretty
much limited baddie power levels to a rank one (two at best) werewolf,
or a 10th gen vampire. Yeah, those are the real hosses of the world of
darkness, all right.

I used to thing Hunter was the worst thing to happen to the World of
Darkness. Then I read Demon.

targets) basically allows for a variety of high-powered effects either
a) very quickly (since standard magick effects take naught but a turn
to resolve) or b) with amazing efficacy (since slower magickal effects
allow for build-ups of successes).

The Sancturary and Node backgrounds, a bit like Allies/Herd in Vampire,
was startling efficient to boosting character prowess, but with far
greater effect.

Without direct GM intervention or a change to canon, a competent player
can pull off staggering effects without incurring paradox using only a
bit of creativity. (Spirit and Mind both afford opportunities to do

rewriting vampiric abilities -- or rewriting magickal ones -- saved
vamires from their agenda.

suggests a lack of invention. A disliked concept more often than not
interferes with invention. I ran and played excellent games of Vampire
where various parts of WW canon were removed because they made better
games, and better ideas, possible. If a bad idea in canon contradicts a
good idea (in canon or otherwise), one throws it out to make a better
game.

But then, there's nothing to indicate that you have any notion that
some propositions prevent the existence of others. For us, if x = 2

pathetic do you have to be to place your personal value on someone
else's gamebook? This is one of the few reasons I can come up with for

were in response to the aforementioned ones.)

Twits aside, the experience in the RPG I had with other players led me
to favor less powerful magic in games with vampires. Actually, I hope
this next set features mortals that have better access to ritual-style
magic (though the "bang! you're on fire" effects of Thaum are cool).
When you take wizards out of the reality-control business, they make
excellent foils/allies of vampires: formidible mortals that you can't
just Discipline your way past. I know Hunters weren't really into the
formal magic thing, but since the WoD story is no longer completely
binding VtES (since WoD "alpha" is discontinued), maybe there's a
chance for additions.

Since the real world has huge, powerful institutions with conflicting

Failure. Of. Imagination.

reiterate, though, I caused you no initial harm and I do hope you work
out whatever personal problems you may have, honestly.You may have the
last word on this, as you seem to need it; I hope it fills whatever
void you have.

allies. I am hoping that the next set has a body of cards specific for
ally types -- ghoul-only actions, mage-only actions (especially those),
werewolf-only. It does run the risk of overpowering allies (as these

vampires interact with mortals all the time, so it would be natural to
have a more diverse body of ally-affecting cards.

I'm pretty interested to see what will come out.
